chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: Five identical SBRs were employed simultaneously throughout the experiment and were numbered SBR-1, SBR-2, SBR-3, SBR-4, and SBR-5, respectively. The operational cycles of the five SBRs processes were similar. The running time of each cycle was 12 h which included 5 time-oriented periodic steps: wastewater filling (5 min), aeration (600 min), settling (90 min), supernatant withdrawal (5 min), and idle (20 min). 2.5 L supernatant wastewater was removed in each cycle. The collected sludge was inoculated into the five SBRs. The excess sludge was discharged periodically to keep the biomass concentration mixedliquor suspended solids (MLSS) stable at approximately 4,500 mg L -1 , and consequently, a hydraulic residence time of 10 d was achieved in each reactor. SBR-1 was used as a control system that was filled with synthetic wastewater without Cu throughout the experiments.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: Water is one of the most important resources for human survival. The water demand has pronounced over the past decades due to population growth, industry development, and agricultural expansion. Although groundwater, surface water, and rainwater are conventional freshwater resources, nowadays, unconventional water resources such as wastewater are recognized as valuable resources for freshwater supply. In this regard, wastewater treatment and reuse have become viable selections for providing additional water supplies (Kim and Jang, 2006) . Membrane bioreactor (MBR) systems are one of the most promising wastewater treatment technologies growing increasingly all over the world, especially in developing countries (Wu et al., 2008) . Membrane bioreactors combine conventional activated sludge (CAS) and membrane separation technologies to produce high-quality water (Zhang et al., 2021) . MBR technology reduces plant footprint by eliminating clarifiers and conventional filters, which makes them more efficient in comparison with conventional wastewater treatment processes (Judd, 2010; Deng et al., 2015) .

chunks.text: It is not necessary to accommodate increases in flow due to storm events because infiltration and inflow do not occur in building systems. The biosolids resulting from anaerobic digestion at the centralized WWTP were assumed to be disposed in equal parts (by mass) via land application and daily cover at a landfill, with transportation requirements and landfill emissions estimated. 19 In reality, the planned treatment process for centralized NPR in San Francisco is more complex and energy-intensive because saltwater intrusion in the sewer system requires reverse osmosis to be implemented for the water used to irrigate parks. For the decentralized treatment process, we evaluated a hypothetical treatment train with a membrane bioreactor (MBR), shown in Figure 2 . Raw wastewater goes through pretreatment (screen filter and a grinder pump to remove solids), a grit chamber, a flow equalization tank, and an MBR for primary and secondary treatment. The effluent is disinfected with UV (primary disinfectant) and chlorine (disinfectant residual) and then stored until needed. The sludge generated from primary and secondary treatment is stored onsite and periodically transported by truck to the closest centralized WWTP for further processing.

chunks.text: SBR is used all over the globe to treat both municipal and industrial wastewater. High-strength wastewater produced from industries like dairy, paper mills, tanneries, and textiles, use SBRs as an alternative treatment process (Suresh et al., 2011) . SBR is a fill and draw system based on the activated sludge process principle. SBR is efficient to treat high pollution load but, requires a high cost of construction as well as high operation and maintenance costs (Mace and Mata-Alvarez, 2002). Aerobic granules based SBRs show good sludge settling properties and are able to achieve constant COD removal of 98% for high-strength wastewater (COD >2500 mg/L) (Hamza et al., 2018) . HRT has a significant role in aerobic granules-based SBRs treatment systems, as sludge settling efficiency improvs with an increase in HRT. The optimum HRT for efficient pollutant removal was observed to be 8 h (X. Wang et al., 2021) .
